extracted.intended_audience: Readers of the New York Tribune; general literate public and lawmakers interested in marriage/divorce law and social reform
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial and published letters debating the proper scope, grounds, and incidental rights associated with divorce and legal separation (New York / Indiana mid-19th-century context). Includes policy prescriptions and descriptions of state law and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve sanctity and perpetuity of Marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The law should maintain the sanctity and perpetuity of Marriage and not freely increase facilities for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial: "We favor whatever may be done to mitigate the hardships endured by mismated persons in perfect consistency with the maintenance of the sanctity and perpetuity of Marriage." The piece urges the Legislature to "ponder long and carefully before it consents" to making divorce easier, arguing marriage should be treated as an irrevocable union and individuals warned to "be very careful how you marry; for a mistake in this regard is irrevocable."

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate hardship while retaining marriage's permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal reforms are warranted to alleviate exceptional hardships of mismated persons so long as they are consistent with preserving marriage as an enduring institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial acknowledges that many persons are badly mated and that "this, we think, is, in the broad view, right, though in special cases it involves hardship." The recommended balance: allow remedies to mitigate suffering but avoid policies that undermine the permanence of marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of property and earnings for women living wholly separate
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman living wholly separate from her husband because of his brutality, cruelty, or profligacy should have the same control over her property and earnings as if she had never married.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial argues the law "ought to allow the woman who is living wholly separate from her husband ... to have the same control over her property and earnings as if she had never married." Example given where the law currently enables a husband to appropriate a wife's earnings; calls for statutory change to make her effectively the legal owner of her earnings while deserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of action for separated wife against culpable third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserted or separated wife should have a legal right of action against culpable third parties (e.g., railroad companies) for injuries to herself, rather than those claims being treated as the husband's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial cites a case where a woman separated from her husband was disabled by a railroad accident yet "the law gives her no right of action against the culpable company; her broken ankles are legally her runaway husband's," emphasizing the injustice and urging change so the deserted wife can sue in her own name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indiana statutory grounds for divorce (as described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indiana law (per Robert Dale Owen) grants divorce for abandonment; for cruel treatment; for habitual drunkenness (he added "habitual drunkenness for two years"); and for any other cause for which the court may deem it proper to grant divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen states he amended the law by adding habitual drunkenness for two years, and that the statute "grants divorce for other causes than the one your law selects, — as for abandonment; for cruel treatment; for habitual drunkenness; and for any other cause for which the court may deem it proper that a divorce should be granted." He defends these grounds as humane and justified by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards for divorce in Indiana: residency and notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A party cannot sue for divorce in Indiana unless they have been a resident for at least one year; provisions regarding timely notice to an absent party are strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen emphasizes that recent changes prevent quick out‑of‑state divorces: "No one can now sue for a divorce in Indiana, until he has been during one year, at least, a resident of the State; and the provision regarding timely notice to the absent party is of the strictest kind." This is presented as corrective of past abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use separation (bed and board) rather than full dissolution for non‑adulatory abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: For many cases of cruelty or brutality, the law should grant a separation from bed and board rather than a complete dissolution of the marriage tie, to prevent permitting the abusive spouse to remarry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley argues: "our laws grant a separation from bed and board, — not a disruption of the marriage tie, with liberty to marry again. I think this is just right. I would not let loose such a wretch ... to delude and torture another 'pure and virtuous girl.'" He presents separation as an appropriate remedy that protects future potential victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution of marriage justified only for adultery (Greeley's view invoking scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage may be rightfully dissolved because of adultery alone (Matthew xix.9); other causes should not justify full dissolution and remarriage, per Greeley's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley cites the New Testament: "His testimony ... is express and unequivocal (Matt. xix. 9), that a marriage can be rightfully dissolved because of adultery alone." He uses this as a moral/legal standard to limit grounds for divorce to adultery if dissolution is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as a lifelong union; substitutes must be named
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is defined as the legal and religious union of a man and a woman for life; if advocates propose an alternative social relation they should set it forth distinctly and not appropriate the name 'marriage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley insists on the classical definition: "Marriage: The act of uniting a man and woman for life ... the mutual and solemn promise to 'take each other for better, for worse' and 'to live together till death do part.'" He argues historical experience favors monogamic lifelong marriage and that any substitute should be given a distinctive name and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divorce as a remedy to preserve the institution when it defeats its purpose (Owen's justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divorce should be available as an exceptional remedy to terminate unions that have degenerated and thus defeat the purpose of marriage, in order to preserve the overall purity and efficacy of the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen writes that he "seek[s] to preserve [marriage's] purity, when other expedients fail, by the besom of divorce" and argues that if marriage becomes "the daily cause of grievous words and heartless deeds... all ought earnestly to seek the most effectual remedy." He frames divorce as corrective for marriages that have become destructive.
